1037.title: Easter Monday
1037.hook: a day for walking, like Emmaus; in some places the Emmaus walk
1037.howItsDone: In some places Christians keep Easter Monday with an Emmaus walk, going out together on foot after the feast, and some churches read Luke's Emmaus story in the days after Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Orthodox Pascha, and a greeting and its answer. Your line was truly he is risen. Where did you hear an answer come back? Day one thousand thirty-seven.

Two friends are already on the road out of Jerusalem, late in the day, heading for a village called Emmaus. They are going over it again and again: the arrest, the cross, and that morning's strange report from some women that the tomb was empty. A stranger falls into step beside them and asks what they're talking about. They stop, faces sad, and one of them, Cleopas, more or less says: are you the only person around here who hasn't heard? The stranger lets them tell the whole thing. Then he starts to talk, and the road gets shorter. In some places, the day after Easter is kept with exactly this: a walk out of town with friends, talking. Today, Easter Monday.

Luke tells this story, and he's careful about one detail: it happens that same day, Easter day itself. So why does a Monday borrow it? Because the morning after a great feast is when ordinary life starts again, and this is a story about Easter turning up on an ordinary road. Watch how it unfolds. In the King James Bible: "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them." But they don't know him. Luke says their eyes were held. He walks the whole way as a stranger, going through Moses and the prophets, explaining the things written about himself. At the village he makes as if to keep walking, and they press him to stay: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent." So he comes in. At the table he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it and hands it to them, and in that moment they know him. Then he's gone from their sight. And here's what they say to each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" They recognized him at the table, but they realize the burning started out on the road. Readers find more than one layer here. Some hear the breaking of bread as an echo of communion. Some hear a picture of the risen Christ walking alongside people who don't yet see him. Others notice the plain hospitality: two tired travelers invite a stranger in at dusk, and that's when everything opens. Then the last turn. They get up that same hour and go all the way back to Jerusalem to tell the others how he was, in Luke's words, "known of them in breaking of bread."
screen: `THAT SAME DAY, ON AN ORDINARY ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a walk with a friend. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you could walk beside this week. Not to fix anything. Just to go somewhere on foot and talk. Picture the route: a park, a block, the long way to the shop. Think of what you might talk about, and then leave a gap, because the Emmaus story happens in the gap nobody planned. If you pray, you can ask that the road be good company. If you don't, just hold that person in mind and look forward to the walk. The bell holds the time.
Easter Monday. The day after Easter, kept in some places with a walk, remembering two friends on the road to Emmaus and the stranger who turned out to be the risen Jesus.
Your line: walk to emmaus. Today, walk somewhere with someone, even a short way, and leave room in the talk for something neither of you planned. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

1038.title: Thomas Sunday
1038.hook: the Sunday after Easter remembers Thomas; Catholics also keep Divine Mercy Sunday
1038.howItsDone: In a number of churches, John 20's story of Thomas is read on the Sunday after Easter; the Orthodox call it Thomas Sunday, and Catholics also keep it as Divine Mercy Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter Monday, and two friends on the road who didn't know who was walking with them. Your line was walk to emmaus. Who did you walk with? Day one thousand thirty-eight.

Thomas was out when it happened. His friends find him and tell him they've seen Jesus alive, and he answers them plainly. In the King James Bible: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe." He isn't rude about it. He just says what it would take. Hands. Nails. Side. Nothing secondhand. For eight days, the story leaves him there, the one in the room who can't say what everyone else is saying. In the Orthodox calendar, the Sunday after Easter is named for him. Today, Thomas Sunday.

John tells it like this: "after eight days again his disciples were within, and Thomas with them." Doors shut. Jesus stands among them and says, "Peace be unto you." Then he turns straight to Thomas and offers him exactly what he asked for: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing." Notice two things. First, Jesus doesn't refuse the request. He answers it, almost word for word. Thomas named his terms, and the risen Jesus meets them. Second, John never says Thomas actually touched him. Some paintings show his finger in the wound, but the text goes straight to what he says: "My Lord and my God." The one who doubted out loud is the one who says it, to Jesus, face to face. Then comes a line meant for everyone who wasn't in that room: "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed." And it's worth knowing who Thomas was before this. Earlier in John, when Jesus decides to go back toward danger, it's Thomas who says to the others, "Let us also go, that we may die with him." The nickname doubting Thomas isn't in the Bible. Some readers would rather call him honest Thomas, or brave Thomas. Churches keep this Sunday in different ways. In the Orthodox calendar it's called Thomas Sunday. Catholics also keep it as Divine Mercy Sunday, a day centered on God's mercy, and some readers hear the two fitting together: a wounded Christ, offering peace, to a friend who couldn't yet believe.

Here's the practice: bring one honest question into the quiet. Settle, and breathe. Let one doubt come up, about faith, or about anything you're asked to trust. Don't argue it down. Don't polish it. Say it to yourself the way Thomas did, plainly, with your terms: this is what it would take. If you pray, you can bring that doubt to God just as it is, the way Thomas said his out loud. If you don't, simply hold the question with a bit of respect, as a sign you're paying attention. The bell holds the time.
Thomas Sunday. The Sunday after Easter, remembering the disciple who said what it would take to believe, and then said, my Lord and my God.
Your line: my lord and my god. Today, when someone asks a hard question, yours or theirs, answer it, or let it stand, instead of shushing it. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

1039.title: Rogation days
1039.hook: villages walk their boundaries praying for the crops
1039.howItsDone: On Rogation days some parishes walk their boundaries in procession, stopping at markers to read scripture and pray for the crops and the community; some city churches walk their streets instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas Sunday: a doubt said out loud, and answered, and then the words my lord and my god. Which honest question did you let stand? Day one thousand thirty-nine.

A stone sits half sunk in a hedge at the edge of a field, letters worn almost smooth. On a set day, in some English villages, a crowd turns up beside it. The priest, the farmers, the old, a gaggle of children carrying long willow sticks. They've been walking since morning, field to field, stopping at every marker that shows where their parish ends and the next begins. At each one, someone reads, someone prays for the crops, and the children whack the stone with their sticks so they'll remember exactly where it is. In the old stories, sometimes it was the children who got bumped on it. The custom has a blunt name: beating the bounds. The days it belongs to have a gentler one. Today, Rogation days.

Tradition explains the name from the Latin for asking, and asking is the whole point. Rogation days are days for asking God for the things a village can't make for itself: rain at the right time, sun at the right time, a harvest. Two old lines fit the day. A psalm, in the King James Bible: "Then shall the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us." And Jesus's plain invitation: "Ask, and it shall be given you." A town that grows its own food knows how little of it is in human hands, and Rogation says so out loud, on foot, in the fields themselves. Then there's the walking of the edges. Why the boundary? Partly memory: the line lived in people's heads, so the young had to see the stones for themselves. But there's a moral edge to it too. Deuteronomy says: "Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance." A boundary stone protects the person on the other side as much as you. Walking it and praying at it is a way of saying: this much is ours to tend, and that much is our neighbor's, and we won't creep. So beating the bounds holds two things together, asking God for enough and honoring where enough ends. Some churches still walk their parish, in the country or around city blocks, praying for the homes, shops and gardens they pass, and for the people who work the land everywhere.

Here's the practice: walk your street's boundary, in your mind first. Settle, and breathe. Start at your own front door. Go to the corner. Picture who lives along the way, the shop, the tree, the patch where something grows. At each corner, stop. If you pray, you can ask for what that stretch needs: work, rest, food on the table, peace between the houses. If you don't, just wish each stretch well as you pass it. Then, later today or this week, walk it for real. The bell holds the time.
Rogation days. Days of asking, when some parishes walk their boundaries, praying for the crops and for the people inside the line and beyond it.
Your line: beating the bounds. Today, notice one boundary you share, a fence, a wall, a desk edge, and do one small fair thing on your neighbor's side of it. Day one thousand thirty-nine.

1040.title: Ascension Day
1040.howItsDone: Churches that keep Ascension Day mark it forty days after Easter with a service reading the end of Luke and the start of Acts; some move the celebration to the following Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rogation days: walking the edges, asking for the harvest. Your line was beating the bounds. Which boundary did you notice, and what did you do on the other side of it? Day one thousand forty.

A small group of friends is standing on a hill outside Jerusalem with their heads tipped back, staring at an empty sky. A moment ago Jesus was talking with them. Then he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. It's the stance of someone left on a platform after the train has gone, still looking at the spot where someone used to be. Then two men in white are standing beside them, and in the King James Bible they ask a fair question: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven?" The book of Acts sets this after forty days of Jesus appearing to his friends. Today, Ascension Day.

Acts begins by saying the risen Jesus was "seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God." That's where the feast's timing comes from. Then the scene on the hill: "while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight." A cloud, in the Bible, can be more than weather. It's how God's presence shows up and hides at once, over the mountain, over the tent in the desert. So the cloud here isn't saying he got lost in the sky. Christians say he went into God's presence. They say it in the old creeds too: he ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. Churches understand that in different ways, some picturing an upward journey, some hearing "up" as the only word we have for going into God. Either way, in the texts it isn't a goodbye. Look how Luke ends his Gospel. After Jesus parts from them, "they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy." Not grief. Joy. Which is odd, until you set it beside Matthew, who doesn't tell the Ascension at all and ends his Gospel with a promise instead: "lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world." The leaving and the promise belong together. Some Christians put it this way: at the Ascension, Jesus stops being in one place so that he can be with his friends everywhere. And then the angels' question does its work. Stop staring up. Go back to the city. There's a wait coming, and then a job. Ascension Day is the feast of looking up, and then getting on with it.

Here's the practice: look up, then get on with it. If you can, go to a window or step outside. Settle, and breathe. Look up for a while. Sky, ceiling, clouds, whatever's there. Let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can hold Matthew's line in the quiet: lo, I am with you alway. If you don't, simply notice the size of the sky over your small day. Then, when the bell comes, bring your eyes down to the next ordinary thing in front of you, and start it. The bell holds the time.
Ascension Day. Forty days after Easter, the feast of Jesus taken up into God's presence, and the promise that he stays with his friends.
Your line: he is with you always. Today, each time you catch yourself staring at what's gone, look up once, then turn back to the next thing in front of you. Day one thousand forty.

1041.title: Pentecost in red
1041.hook: churches wear red, some read Acts in many languages at once
1041.howItsDone: At Pentecost some churches use red vestments and decorations, and some invite readers to read Acts 2 aloud in several languages at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ascension Day: a cloud, a hill, and friends told to stop staring at the sky. Your line was he is with you always. What did you turn back to? Day one thousand forty-one.

The reader steps up to the lectern on Pentecost Sunday and starts the story in English. A moment later a second voice joins in, in Spanish. Then a third, in Korean. A fourth, in Swahili. A fifth, in something the person in the third row can't place at all. For a few seconds the church is a wonderful mess of sound, nobody quite following, some catching their own language somewhere in the noise. Look around and the room has gone red: red stoles, red banners, people in red shirts and red scarves. Some churches do exactly this, on purpose. They're acting out a story. Today, Pentecost in red.

The story is in the second chapter of Acts. Jesus's friends are together in one room, waiting, as they were told to. In the King James Bible: "suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them." That's the red. Fire, resting on each person. Then they begin "to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Notice the word doing double duty. Tongues of fire on their heads; tongues, meaning languages, in their mouths. Out in the street, a crowd of people from many nations gathers, baffled, because, as Acts puts it, "every man heard them speak in his own language." They ask, "how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" Notice what doesn't happen. The Spirit doesn't hand everyone one shared language. Nobody has to give up their mother tongue to understand. Each person hears good news in the words they grew up with. Some readers hear an answer to the tower of Babel, where languages scattered people: here the languages stay, and people are gathered anyway. Not everybody's impressed, by the way. Some in the crowd mock and say they're "full of new wine." That's why some churches read Acts in several languages at once on this day: the jumble is the point. And it's why the red. Acts tells this as the day the Spirit came like fire, and churches that keep the color dress the room to look like it.
screen: `TONGUES ON THEIR HEADS, AND IN THEIR MOUTHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wear something red, or hold something red. A sock, a pen, a mug, a scarf. Settle, and breathe. Let the color stand for the fire in the story. Now bring to mind someone whose first language isn't yours: a neighbor, a coworker, a shopkeeper, a grandparent. Think of the words they grew up with, the ones they pray or curse or sing in. If you pray, you can hold that person before God in their own tongue, even if you don't know a word of it. If you don't, just honor the language they carry. The bell holds the time.
Pentecost in red. The feast of the Spirit coming like wind and fire in Acts, when churches dress in red and some read the story in many languages at once.
Your line: every tongue. Today, learn how to say thank you in someone else's language, and use it on them. Day one thousand forty-one.

1042.title: Trinity Sunday
1042.hook: the one Sunday for the mystery at the heart of it all
1042.howItsDone: On Trinity Sunday some churches sing hymns to the Trinity and say a creed, and preachers often take up the texts where Father, Son and Spirit are named together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecost in red: wind, fire, and a crowd hearing the news in the languages they were born with. Your line was every tongue. Whose thank you did you learn? Day one thousand forty-two.

There's a legend told about Augustine, the North African bishop and writer. He's walking along a beach, turning a hard question over and over: how can God be one, and also three? He comes across a child who has dug a little hole in the sand and is running back and forth to the sea with a shell, pouring water into the hole. Augustine asks what he's doing. Putting the sea in this hole, says the child. Augustine laughs: that's impossible. And the child answers, more or less, so is fitting God into your head. Nobody needs the legend to be true for it to land. After the run of Easter and Pentecost, the church calendar keeps one Sunday just for that question. Today, Trinity Sunday.
screen: `THE SEA IN A HOLE IN THE SAND.`

segments.voice: Start with one God. Moses says it in Deuteronomy, in the King James Bible: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD." Jesus quotes it himself when he's asked which commandment comes first. Christians hold on to that line. And yet the Gospels keep naming three together. At Jesus's baptism, in Matthew, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and a voice from heaven says, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Father speaking, Son in the water, Spirit descending, all in one scene. At the very end of Matthew, Jesus sends his friends out "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Some Christian readers point out that it says the name, not the names. And Paul signs off a letter: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." Over time the church found a word for what these texts hold together: Trinity. One God, Christians who hold the creeds say, in three persons. Not three gods. Not one God wearing three masks. Father, Son and Spirit, each fully God, and one. Then comes a caution. Some teachers in the tradition say that every picture for this falls short. Shamrocks, water and ice and steam: they help a little, and then they leak. That's why Christians call it a mystery. In Christian use, a mystery isn't a puzzle waiting for a clever answer. It's something held to be true that you can live inside without ever getting to the bottom of. The sea doesn't fit in the hole. People still swim in it.
screen: `THE LORD OUR GOD IS ONE LORD.`
`FATHER, SON AND SPIRIT IN ONE SCENE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a mystery. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to solve anything. Bring to mind something you know is true but can't fully explain. The way a parent loves three children completely. Why a piece of music can bring someone to tears. What a person is, really, behind the face. Stay with it, without explaining it. If you pray, you can rest in Paul's farewell: the grace of Christ, the love of God, the communion of the Spirit. If you don't, simply let the big thing stay big, and sit beside it. The bell holds the time.
Trinity Sunday. The Sunday after Pentecost, kept for the Christian belief in one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit: in Christian words, a mystery to live inside, not a puzzle to solve.
Your line: three in one. Today, when you meet something you can't explain, resist tidying it up, and let it stay a little bigger than you. Day one thousand forty-two.

1043.title: Corpus Christi
1043.hook: Catholics carry the sacrament through the streets in procession
1043.howItsDone: On Corpus Christi some Catholic parishes carry the consecrated host in a monstrance through the streets under a canopy, with hymns, candles and stops for prayer along the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Trinity Sunday: the sea that won't fit in a hole in the sand. Your line was three in one. What did you let stay bigger than you? Day one thousand forty-three, and the end of a week.

A small bell rings at the corner, and the street goes quiet. Down the middle of the road, over a carpet of flower petals someone spent all night laying out, comes a procession: children in white, a band, people carrying candles, and under a canopy held up on poles, a priest holding something gold and shining in both hands. In its center is a small round wafer of bread. As it passes, people on the sidewalk kneel. A man stops on his bike and takes off his cap. A shopkeeper steps out of her doorway to watch. This happens in some Catholic towns and parishes on one feast, and the feast's name is just two Latin words. Today, Corpus Christi.
screen: `A BELL, AND THE STREET GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: Corpus Christi is Latin for the body of Christ. The words go back to the night before Jesus died. Paul passes them on in a letter, in the King James Bible: Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said, "this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me." In John's Gospel Jesus says, "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." Christians have understood those words in more than one way. Catholic teaching holds that at Mass the bread truly becomes the body of Christ, and that he remains present in it afterward. So the consecrated host can be kept, honored and carried, and on this feast it's taken out of the church and through the streets. Orthodox Christians also speak of the bread truly becoming Christ's body, though this procession belongs to the Western calendar, and some Anglican churches mark the day too. Other Protestants understand communion as a remembrance, or as Christ present by the Spirit to those who receive it, and wouldn't carry the bread in procession. Each takes the words seriously. They hear them differently. Here's what the procession itself says, for those who keep it. What happens at the altar isn't meant to stay behind the church doors. It goes past the bakery, the bus stop, the apartments with laundry on the balconies. That fits the week we've just walked. Two friends on the road to Emmaus, who knew him in the breaking of bread. A parish walking its boundaries. A crowd in the street hearing the news in their own languages. Again and again this week, the holy went outside.

Here's the practice: walk your streets in your mind, one stop at a time, the way a procession pauses. Settle, and breathe. This time, don't start from your own door. Start with the busiest place you pass in an ordinary week: a station, a supermarket line, a school gate. Bring the crowd there to mind, the faces you half know. Then a quieter place: a bench, a laundromat, a clinic waiting room. Then the place you'll be tonight. If you pray, you can pray for the people in each place, the way the procession blesses the streets it moves through. If you don't, simply hold each place as if it mattered, because to someone it does. The bell holds the time.
